power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Repurposing, redefining, and reimagining: A paradigm shift towards person-driven neuroscience in the digital age

text.text: The focus of neuroscience has traditionally hinged on collecting quantifiable physiological data that are often distanced from the lived experiences of people.
In contrast, qualitative, subjective, and situational information provides rich context, but lacks the empirical precision needed to map to neural processes.
To reconcile this gap, we established 'The Lαβ' as an interdisciplinary initiative that fuses person-driven experiences, personal reflection, and empirical neuroscience.
People engage with their chosen experiences in their chosen settings while wearing a portable EEG headset.
Timestamped information is then collected from a variety of sources.

We introduce our novel neurotriangulation approach: A person-driven synthesis of quantitative electrophysiological signals, qualitative observations, and subjective and situational information into a single analytic stream.
Our aim is to provide people with opportunities for neuro-self-reflection.
We use an ethicsfirst approach to preserve data sovereignty, privacy, autonomy, and agency for the individual.
In this paper, we present real-world case studies to demonstrate our data collection, real-time field analysis, and cointerpretation methodologies.
These case studies also underscore the neurotriangulation model as an approach to move beyond reductive, data-centric models toward a person-driven paradigm.
This shift allows neurodata to be more accessible, inclusive, and personally meaningful, while prioritising safety and subjectivity.
This has the potential to reshape how we think about neuroscientific applications in fields such as education and training, anthropology, creative arts, wellbeing, and mental health.
By repurposing and redefining the use of extant neurotechnology, we are reimagining a future in which our understanding of ourselves is person-driven, reality-based, and ethically sound.
Technological repurposing has frequently precipitated profound paradigm shifts.

A salient example of this is the origins of turntablism, when the traditional phonograph record player was repurposed to create new sounds and breakbeats thereby laying the foundational sonic architecture of hip-hop.
This movement signified a decisive reconfiguration of technology use, which catalysed the emergence of a new genre and subsequent global surge of music production and consumption (References 1-2).

Likewise, Eddie Van Halen's modification of a deconstructed Fender Stratocaster to create new sounds exemplifies how the reimagining of a stock instrument redefined the parameters of rock music (Reference 3).

In both cases, the repurposing of extant technology not only broadened the expressive vocabulary of their respective genres, but also profoundly altered and evolved the cultural understanding of what constitutes musical artistry.
Recent technological advances in consumer-grade electroencephalography (EEG) equipment have enabled neurodata acquisition outside of traditional clinical and neuroscience settings.
This emerging capability to extract multimodal quantitative raw data from commercially available EEG headsets has acted as a catalyst for our proposed paradigm shift in how neuroscience is used.
We established 'The Lαβ' (Reference 4), an interdisciplinary initiative that fuses person-driven experiences, personal reflection, and empirical neuroscience.
The Lαβ facilitates people to engage with their chosen experiences in their chosen settings while being brain scanned using a portable EEG headset.

We began in 2021 with simple data acquisition protocols that progressively evolved into sophisticated real-time methodologies and field analyses that integrate qualitative observations, subjective and situational knowledge, and quantitative metrics.
We refer to our approach as 'neurotriangulation'.

By repurposing the raw data derived from EEG headsets and by distancing ourselves from commercially driven neurotechnological agendas and from clinical and research settings, we have initiated a paradigm shift that empowers individuals to explore their own neural dynamics at a pace and in a manner that has meaning to them.
We argue that this allows neurodata to be more accessible and inclusive, giving people a new lens for deepening self-reflection.

In this paper, we outline our model and methodologies, the conceptual and ethical underpinnings of The Lαβ, and the implications of this shift for safely reimagining the future potential of neuro-self-exploration.
We adopt a new term called 'neurotriangulation'.
In various configurations, our model merges available quantitative, qualitative, and subjective and situational data modalities with millisecond timestamped precision.
We engage with the people we scan to interpret these data.
We can do real-time field analysis to explore immediate insights, and/or look more deeply into the data after further reflection and additional processing.
People's chosen experiences vary tremendously, and we outline some high-level themes in Supplementary Table 1.
text.formatted: People's chosen experiences vary tremendously, and we outline some high-level themes in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Our approach prioritises people's comfort levels and their chosen experiences, especially when collecting extremely sensitive personal information.
The person being scanned always chooses how we collect data and what methodologies we use, leading to more authentic data, based on trust, mutual respect, and boundaries.
We take an 'ethics-first' approach.
People we scan are by default treated anonymously.
Data sovereignty is essential, so people are always in full control of their own data.
We respect people's privacy, agency, and their mental liberty.
We have established continuous informed consent procedures, and we adapt our approaches to different contexts and cultures (Reference 5-6).
As people choose what data should and should not be collected, the types and amounts of data we collect varies tremendously.
We have an array of novel approaches for collecting and documenting meaningful data:
Qualitative observations are descriptive, non-numerical records of what is seen, heard, or experienced during the person's experience.
Qualitative observations are being increasingly used in healthcare (Reference 7).
The Lαβ refers to qualitative observations as 'Qual Notes'.

We have a wide range of approaches and methods for recording Qual Notes, which can be collected at any time: In advance of having the brain scanning experience while talking through their ideas; before the brain scan session starts; during their brain scan; and after their experiences (post-scan follow-ups).
Qual Notes we have collected range from one brief experience, to across multiple days or even years of continued engagement.
We also collect descriptive 'Numerical Qual Notes', which are observations of changes in a person's brain wave activity.
We refer to this as 'brain annotation'.
This can be done in real time or by using screen recording video playbacks.
When we observe brain wave changes in real time, we refer to this as 'Play Mode'.
This involves using a smartphone to visualise five brain waves aggregated across multiple brain regions.
We can also annotate in 'Complex Play Mode', which is essentially the disaggregated version of Play Mode.
Whenever possible, our Qual Notes are timestamped.
Qual Note data collection can be done discreetly, or even collectively with multiple people taking 'Group Qual Notes'.

Examples of the types of Qual Notes we have documented include: "6:18 minutes -person takes a drink of water (pulls it out from his bag I think)" followed by "6:26 min person spontaneously started to sing!!!!".
We can screen grab images of the Play Mode brainwaves at various points during their scan, and these can be linked with text-tagged qualitative observations.
Overall, we have an array of options for recording Qual Notes, including abstract tagging, audio and text capture.
We are agnostic with regards to the methods we use, choosing whatever is most appropriate in context with the person and their experience.
Subjective observations arise from personal feelings, opinions, and beliefs.
Situational information is a person's context and circumstances.
The Lαβ views subjective and situational information as legitimate data and believes that people's knowledge about themselves enriches (neuro)triangulation with qualitative and quantitative data.
We consider this to be a new field called 'Neuroethnology'.
We document first-person perspectives and situational information in a similar way to our Qual Notes.
Furthermore, we use cultural competency approaches (for example, people have chosen to sing and/or listen to a song in different native languages) to enable deeper, more nuanced insights.
Quantitative data involves numerical measurements and statistical methods.
The Lαβ has the capability to collect diverse multimodal data, including heart rate, brain wave activity, head motion, video, and audio.
We have two main ways of collecting neurodata.
One is by taking screen recordings of the real-time brain waves we see in Play Mode.
We can also collect full granular neurodata in a '.csv' file format.
We call this a 'Deep Dive'.
We always prioritise the person's experience over 'perfect' EEG signals.
For example, if the headset shifts, we don't interrupt the person to adjust it.
When signal drop-out is observed in Play Mode, this is timestamped in the Qual Notes, to help with the co-analysis of the resulting data, and avoid spurious associations.
We now describe an example of neurotriangulation, using the experience of a person we scanned, named Charlie.
By default, we keep people anonymous, but Charlie has given us permission to use her name, and to use her 'Project Beaumont Dance Crew' as an example.
For context, Charlie leads dance classes for elderly people in low resource settings and founded The Blair Academy, a social enterprise centred on supporting healthy ageing through hip-hop dance.
Data collection for this project began in 2023 and remains ongoing.
Before Charlie had her scan, she provided us with subjective and situational information about a video she created that she wanted to watch while being scanned.
This acted as our 'entry point' into her chosen experience (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: This acted as our 'entry point' into her chosen experience (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: She told us that she believed that her brain would "definitely change" at a specific point while she watched herself in her video.
She even played this part of the video for us in advance so that we were prepared when making our Qual Notes and watching her brain waves in Play Mode.
Charlie created her video because her dance class funding was coming to an end and she wanted to share this video with her funders hoping they would extend her funding.
Quantitative outputs were mapped to Qual Notes and video descriptives from the video she watched.
At her predicted point in the video, we observed a sudden reduction in all of Charlie's brain waves (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: At her predicted point in the video, we observed a sudden reduction in all of Charlie's brain waves (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

text.text: Around this time, in Charlie's video she is saying "When these sessions end…ahhh, it's hard for me to even say because it makes me feel emotional.
I don't like to think about them coming to an end because what we've created here is such a beautiful community and I'll be really sad to see that go".
The sudden change in her brain waves occurs when she is saying "it makes me feel emotional…".

After Charlie had finished her experience and she had left, we were able to reobserve her quantitative data in more depth and make additional Numerical Qual Notes, using this as our own separate entry point (Figure 1C).
text.formatted: After Charlie had finished her experience and she had left, we were able to reobserve her quantitative data in more depth and make additional Numerical Qual Notes, using this as our own separate entry point (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

text.text: We had collected a video screen recording of her brain waves while she watched her chosen video.
For each of the five brain waves, we were able to identify a global maximum and global minimum.

For example, Charlie's global maximum for her theta brain wave occurred at a specific time point in the video and we were able to use this neurodata timestamp to identify what words were being said by Charlie in her video at that time.
Charlie was speaking about someone named "Elsa".

We contacted Charlie to ask who Elsa is, and she provided additional subjective and situational information, explaining that Elsa gathered the community together to attend Charlie's classes, and that "she's the glue of the community".
Approximately one month after Charlie had her first brain scan experience with us, she told us that she had secured additional funding to lead more dance classes.
She requested to be scanned again while she re-watched the original video (that she watched during her first scan).

Our entry point for this neurotriangulation is her rewatching the same video after having provided us with her subjective and situational information about the positive change in her funding (Figure 2A).
text.formatted: Our entry point for this neurotriangulation is her rewatching the same video after having provided us with her subjective and situational information about the positive change in her funding (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>).

text.text: In the previous scan we only had Play Mode data, but for this follow-up scan we were able to record full neurodata (a Deep Dive) as illustrated in Figure 2B.
text.formatted: In the previous scan we only had Play Mode data, but for this follow-up scan we were able to record full neurodata (a Deep Dive) as illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>.

text.text: When we analysed this quantitative data, one of the things we observed was a substantial increase in right frontal lobe activity at two specific times.

Looking back at the video, at the first of these, Charlie is speaking about funding (Figure 2C), and at the second, the video is displaying her funder's logo and showing written words of gratitude (Figure 2D).
text.formatted: Looking back at the video, at the first of these, Charlie is speaking about funding (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2C</ref>), and at the second, the video is displaying her funder's logo and showing written words of gratitude (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2D</ref>).

text.text: Charlie affirmed that these quantitative and qualitative insights aligned with her subjective and situational perspective and she gave us additional new insights to further triangulate.
Taken altogether, Charlie's neurotriangulation examples empirically map her experiences, ranging from financial uncertainty and emotional distress to financial resilience, security, and stability.

These examples demonstrate that the entry points for neurotriangulation can come from any of the data modalities and can occur in any configuration or set of configurations depending on the person's journey.
Together with EEG brain activity, other quantitative data can enhance neurotriangulation.

In another case study, which we call 'Project Love Story', not only do we see brain wave changes across experiences (for example, singing a love song versus thinking about gaming), but we also observe changes in heart rate and head motion (Supplementary Figure 1).
text.formatted: In another case study, which we call 'Project Love Story', not only do we see brain wave changes across experiences (for example, singing a love song versus thinking about gaming), but we also observe changes in heart rate and head motion (Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Using our Qual Notes we were able to validate that the person moved their head a lot while singing, and much less during the instrumental parts of the song.
We provide additional multimodal case study examples of 'Deep Dive' data in Supplementary Figures 2 3 4.
text.formatted: We provide additional multimodal case study examples of 'Deep Dive' data in Supplementary Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> <ref type="figure">3</ref> <ref type="figure">4</ref>.

text.text: In brief, these relate to experiences in which people were: writing while reflecting on how to balance different approaches in their life, listening to their domestic violence "anthem" song (and spontaneously deciding to dance), and listening to an inspirational song.
The data we collect is inherently noisy.
We implement validation strategies to address this when possible.
For example, we can calibrate heart rate data from the EEG headset with medical grade equipment.
We also timestamp otherwise insignificant information in our Qual Notes to check that our timings map (e.g., noting the time when a particular lyric occurs in a song).
Subjective and situational validation is integrated through our neurotriangulation model.
People have made personal observations about their behaviours either during their experience or while co-interpreting their data afterwards.

For example, one person flagged up the importance of a very brief yet precise moment in their head motion data that was statistically invisible yet held tremendous psychological significance to that person.
If it matters to the person, then it is significant.
In another example, we sent a headset overseas and remotely trained a person to scan themselves.
Later, they told us that they spontaneously started to dance while listening to a very emotional song related to a past relationship involving domestic violence.
This information mapped to striking increases in head motion data (Supplementary Figure 3).
text.formatted: This information mapped to striking increases in head motion data (Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: This was important given that we were not present with the person and could not take Qual Notes.

Furthermore, we were able to use the head motion data to identify the part of the song in which the person started dancing, which further enriched our co-analysis and co-interpretation of their experience.

As much as we can attempt to validate our data sources, it is important to note that working with neurodata is not a precise science, especially given the complexities of the human brain (Reference 8).
Even in neuroscientific research, computational models can be fallible, and analyses can be misinterpreted as a result (Reference 9).

Different methods of analysis can arrive at different conclusions, even when controlling for testing the same data set (personal communication), and researcher experience and data quality affect the reproducibility of findings (Reference 10).
We want to address the illusion of control with quantitative data, and distance ourselves from the notion of 'the more data the better'.
Our person-specific approach acknowledges and allows for vagueness and imprecise information, and we are always transparent about this with the people we scan.
Our real-world neurotriangulation approach offers adaptable methodologies for neuro-self-reflection.
Rather than diagnostic, prescribed, or predictive profiling, we are observing life.
We are not conducting clinical trials nor are we trying to modify people's behaviours with interventions.
We are not testing hypotheses or implying causality.
We do not remove outliers and instead deal with the reality of what is collected.
Data artefacts matter to us, and we value the importance of features that might otherwise be omitted in research (e.g., jaw clenching).
We are equipment agnostic and map real life in pragmatic ways.

We are transmogrifying the laboratory into the lived environment, and performing person-specific analyses to examine nuanced, within-person associations that are often obscured in aggregated group-level studies.
We believe that 'richness of data' represents the importance and meaning attributed to human experiences.

Unsolicited feedback has described our approach as "healing", "cathartic", "affirming", "magical" and that our "...brain scans open up such possibilities for people to 'communicate' their emotions in ways that may be hard for them in the traditional sense" (Supplementary Table 2).
text.formatted: Unsolicited feedback has described our approach as "healing", "cathartic", "affirming", "magical" and that our "...brain scans open up such possibilities for people to 'communicate' their emotions in ways that may be hard for them in the traditional sense" (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: We are collaborating with an academic group who have obtained ethical approval for ongoing research examining our impact.
We have observed that people's chosen experiences often connect with mental health themes.
For example, choosing to sing the chorus of an eating disorder safety song, or performing body percussion drumming on their chest to heavy metal music to help their ADHD.
We are safely exploring how our approach could act as a support tool for neuro-selfreflection, wellbeing, mental health, and clinical care (e.g., in psychiatry, neurology, and oncology).
We will continue to support creative arts applications that make neuroexperiences accessible in everyday life.
For example, we used our Play Mode neurodata as a creative tool to help judge a UK Rap Battle and observed the impact of each rapper on our brain waves to assist with decision-making (Reference 11).
This example can be extended to numerous social settings and situations.
We will continue to develop collaborations within education, training, and academic settings.

For example, building upon our brain scanning collaborations in South Africa (Reference 5-6, 12) we will continue to support research and student development by running workshops, co-creating training manuals, and adapting guidance about our approach so it can be used by others to support local communities in culturally sensitive ways.
Our empirical approach can also strengthen evidence in other fields, such as neurophenomenology.
This field has faced many challenges and limitations (Reference 13) but can be enhanced by linking first-person experiences with neurodata, especially in real-world settings.
The Lαβ has ongoing and future goals planned in various directions, including our own internal research and design developments.

In parallel to hardware expansion, our software stack is being enhanced with automated audio-analysis and cross-modal alignment tools, allowing us to map spoken content and ambient sounds onto the neural timeline without manual coding.
This will enable us to integrate richer phenomenological accounts to bridge first-person experiences with objective metrics.

We initially constrained our neurodata to only frontal and temporal channels so that we could validate the neurotriangulation model, but future work will expand brain coverage and brain-related metrics.
Over the course of almost five years, our findings have provided insights into how neural processes interact with contextual variables, social dynamics, cultural norms, and environmental factors.
We have performed numerous pop-up scanning events in multiple countries, demonstrating feasibility, adaptability, and acceptability.
We believe that the repurposing of extant neurotechnology not only expands the uses of neuroscience but also reshapes the cultural conception of what constitutes the field itself.
Figure 1A:
In this example of neurotriangulation, Charlie's entry point was when she decided to watch a video that she had created, which had strong subjective and situational meaning to her.
Before watching the video, she informed us of a precise moment while watching the video when her brain would 'crash'.
The 'Play Mode' real-time brain wave data confirmed this change as shown in Figure 5.
text.formatted: The 'Play Mode' real-time brain wave data confirmed this change as shown in Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>.

text.text: The two images above are screenshots from two separate videos that were then played and recorded simultaneously in a timestamped sensitive manner to create the combined video above.
The left image relates to Charlie's brain waves recorded in real-time while she watched a very meaningful video that she had created (right screenshot).
During this 25 second combined video, at the 13-second point we observed notable changes in Charlie's brain waves.
At this time, in Charlie's video she is saying: "it makes me feel emotional…".
For a broader temporal and linguistic context, from 7 seconds to 22 seconds Charlie says: "When these sessions end…ahhh, it's hard for me to even say because it makes me feel emotional.
I don't like to think about them coming to an end because what we've created here is such a beautiful community and I'll be really sad to see that go".

The left image relates to a phone video screen recording of Charlie's brain activity, which is aggregated data across brain regions in real-time (we refer to this approach as 'Play Mode', which allows for in-the-moment brain activity monitoring).

Charlie's brain activity was being recorded while she watched the full 10:50 minutes long video she created: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEoHKLlvWB8) that she had chosen for her brain scan experience.
text.formatted: Charlie's brain activity was being recorded while she watched the full 10:50 minutes long video she created: <ref type="url" target="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEoHKLlvWB8">https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEoHKLlvWB8</ref>) that she had chosen for her brain scan experience.

text.text: Prior to being scanned she voluntarily disclosed more context.
Charlie leads free street dance sessions with elderly communities on council estates in London, UK.
She explained that her dance classes were running out of funding and so she created her video to share with her funders.

Before the brain scanning started, Charlie voluntarily told me that around the 9:00-minute point (of her watching her own video) her brain would change as it's a very emotional part of the video for her, she said (her hypothesis, not ours).
This corresponds with when she said: "When these sessions end…".
In this example, when we (The Lab) explored Charlie's brain waves outside of the time she said her brain would change, we observed timestamped global maximums and minimums for all 5 brain waves.
For example, we noted that her theta wave peaked to a maximum much earlier in her video.
When we used the brain timestamp to then re-watch the video at that time, Charlie mentions someone named 'Elsa'.
When we asked Charlie who Elsa was, she said: "Ahh, Elsa, she's the glue of the community.
She's the one that helped bring everyone together".
Figure 2A:

In this example, the entry point for neurotriangulation relates to when Charlie contacted us a month after her first scan to inform us that she had since managed to secure additional funding from the same funder and that she wanted to be brain scanned again while re-watching the same video she had watched previously, but this time from a very positive state of mind about money and funding success.
Charlie made no predictions about her brain waves for this follow-up brain scan unlike her first scan.
We were unable to co-analyse the data in real-time on this occasion, but we collected a 'Deep Dive' cvs file.

When we analysed the data and created the 'Trends Plot' as shown in Figure 7 we noticed very visible increased right frontal lobe activation ('yellow blobs') seen very clearly twice during the video Charlie watched.

text.text: Charlie wanted to re-watch the same video she had previously created for the funding body, but this time from a positive state of mind knowing she secured additional funding (in contrast to when her funding was previously coming to an end).
For Charlie's follow-up scanning session we had access to raw brain wave output data unlike the aggregated 'Play Mode' screen video recording that was only available for her previous scan.
This time we were able to record the raw data as a csv file for a deeper analysis of all brain wave trend data for each of the four lobes (bilateral frontal and temporal lobes).
Figure 2B shows two areas where the right frontal lobe (yellow line) has strong activation starting at: 226 (Figure 2C below) and at 635 (Figure 2D below).

text.text: In summary, we observed changes in right frontal lobe activity when Charlie had re-watched this section of her video specifically related to her funders and partnerships.
Painting; dancing; instrument playing; improvisation; music learning; singing; moulding clay into art while blind folded; reading a film pitch to a director; being a cypher judge at a rap battle.
Freestyle rapping; reflecting on receiving funds to help disadvantaged groups.
Expressing struggles with aphasia; grappling with isolation and loneliness.
Working on brain challenge puzzles; episodic future thinking and planning; thinking about education and future career choices, reading an academic paper.
Scrolling on different social media platforms; digital screen drawing.
Music collaborative experiences; new cross-cultural experiences; thinking about their relationship; feeding animals; hugging a friend.
Walking around and interacting with people you know in your community; scanning people in community centres.
Performing squats and other gym routine exercises, watching a video of himself doing a back flip for the first time and a slam dunk for the first time, balancing while imagining snowboarding.

text.text: Project Love Story: A robotics undergraduate student chose multiple experiences to reflect on, some of which relate to data shown above.
He explained in advance that he was on the cusp of entering into a new romantic relationship.
Related to this, for one of his chosen experiences he decided to sing while playing a Chinese love song.
He then played another love song afterwards imagining what their future could be like together and how their lives could be like a modern Romeo and Juliet with a happy ending as the song suggests.
1A shows his brain activity during the 2 love songs, which corresponds with increased activity in the right frontal lobe (shown in yellow above) as timestamped with the onset and ending of each song.
We observed gyroscopic differences with a sharp increase observed when he was singing versus not singing.

After the love song scans, he wanted to be scanned while he was listening to a gaming song that really excited him called "Legends Never Die" and while nostalgia scrolling on his phone viewing gaming avatars.
In 1A, we observed a sharp contrast in the gaming-related experience data observations with increased left frontal lobe activity (shown in red above).
1B shows data only for the first love song while he was singing most of the time.
Our qualitative notes timestamped when he was singing versus not singing.
We observed that when he was not singing his gyroscopic movements were lower and when he was singing the gyroscopic activity increased.

We observed that the brain data around the 425 mark (7 minutes into his full set of scans) is mainly the right frontal lobe (yellow; AF8) with some left frontal lobe (red; AF7) to a much smaller extent.
Notably, the brain waves visually appear as a thin yet slightly bumpy line.
We re-analysed the data, for example, focusing only between 426.50 -427.50 (7 minutes 6.5 second-point for one second) as shown in a much more granular visualisation in 1C.

Overall, this project contains extremely detailed sources of qualitative information (his subjectiveness, our qualitative notes, music, lyrics etc.) that can be mapped at different quantitative resolutions, to see a spectrum or very large differences, such as thinking about romance versus gaming, but also extremely granular trends based on our neurotriangulation methodologies.

text.text: Project Balance: one of our international pop-ups in South Africa (June 2025) included scanning choir members from The Cape Malay Choir Board.
One person we scanned wanted to reflect on finding balance within his life.
He chose to write in his notebook and to internally reflect for over 40 minutes.

He consented for me to make timestamped qualitative observations during his session, such as words he was writing, when he paused from writing, and noting interesting changes in his real-time captured brain wave data.
He voluntarily disclosed subjective information before, during, and after his session that was all documented.

For example, he mentioned that he wanted to reflect on two different ways to approach his life moving forward while also making past and present reflections, and how he wanted to find a balance point in his life between 'active and focused' and 'relaxed' states and then ultimately hoping to find his 'centre'.
We observed changes in heart rate, brain wave data in four brain regions (bilateral frontal and temporal lobes), and head motion data across his session.
Most strikingly, we observed changes in brain wave activity in the right frontal lobe as visualized in yellow ('AF8' in the legend), which aligned with reductions in gyroscopic head motion.
Furthermore, for example around the 1500-seconds point (25 minutes into his scan) we observed changes in brain wave activity in the left frontal lobe as visualized in red ('AF7' in the legend).
We can observe this change between left and right frontal lobes more than once and with more granular analysis.
Many more observations were made when combining quantitative, qualitative, and subjective data sources.
We have a very contextualised set of qualitative notes for this project, which helped us to make more data insights with him.
For this project, we remotely collaborated with someone we have never met in-person who is based overseas outside of the UK.
We posted one of our headsets and remotely taught this person how to scan their own brain in the privacy of their own chosen places and times.
This person self-scanned while engaging in numerous chosen activities over the course of several weeks.
With informed consent they allowed us to analyse the data and discuss it with them safely and securely remotely.
For example, the figure above is data derived when the person chose to listen to a song that had deep meaning to them called: "Love The Way You Lie" by EMINEM featuring Rihanna.
It is this person's domestic violence survival anthem related to a previous partner.
The person told us about the song's meaning: "…it was kind of an anthem song for me during that time...
I listened to it again, to remember how I felt and what I remembered from my clinical experience.
Music is just so powerful, and I have always known that intuitively.
I can't wait to see what it does to my brain.
It felt like a great release.
I even had to dance....it was involuntary!".
For this particular scanning session, the person gave us unprompted subjective knowledge about how they spontaneously chose to dance while listening to the song.
This helped us to understand the data better, especially given that we had not been present for any scans to make any qualitative or real-time quantitative observations.
Their subjective information helped toward validating certain aspects of the data set.
We observed significant increases in head motion and heart rate toward the end of the song and scan when she danced.
We have not included brain data in this Figure above given how sensitive their chosen experience was.

text.text: Project Impossible Dream.
This is someone listening to a song that is deeply inspirational and motivating to them for over 30 years called "Impossible Dream" by Luther Vandross.
The song lyrics remind her of her desire to serve humanity and the greater good (without being religious herself).

Specifically, she said the way Luther Vandross sings 'for that heavenly cause' in a drawn-out way, especially the word 'cause', always elicits something from within her that feels liberating, freeing, and very empowering.
4A shows data while she listened to the full song.
4B is the same image but zoomed in showing a small amount of yellow (between 150 -200; 2:30 -3:20 min), which is hard to see in 4A.
4C is an analysis that only captures 165 -170 (2:45 -2:50 min), which is the only time yellow is visible throughout the song.
The yellow corresponds with the right frontal lobe (AF8), which is only activated when the artist sings: 'for that heavenly cause'.
The Lαβ has engaged in a wide range of thematic scanning.
Some examples of people's chosen experiences (high-level description; nuance not shown)

Emotional, meditative activities; internal reflection; personal expression; singing and/or listening to a song in different native languages; speaking and singing in tongues; reflecting on connections and relationships with self and others; playing Native American flute; reading religious scriptures out loud and feeling grounded by it.

Mindful breathing; eating favourite and least favourite foods; talking about their recent engagement and family reactions; Kung fu and Tai Chi to help address menopause brain fog; looking at family holiday photos, watching videos of their child play sports at an elite level.

Listening to music, singing, or dancing while reflecting on experiences related to mental health such as a previous suicide attempt, social anxiety, eating disorder, domestic violence, past trauma, losing a loved one, reflecting on a near death drowning experience.
Contrasting life events and relationships over long periods of time using multiple scans.

Community support for low-income settings; navigating unexpected emotional interactions with someone; reflecting on being adopted; hugging a friend while imagining it is their loved one overseas, listening to music related to a recent break-up.
Listening to music that evoked old memories; wanting to talk about their past life history; looking through decades of old photos.
